hook_text: Burn something and it should get lighter. Burn magnesium and it gets heavier. Here is why.
clip_script: Burn a piece of wood and you are left with a little ash, so you might think burning always makes things lighter. Now hold a strip of magnesium ribbon in a flame. It bursts into a dazzling white light, too bright to stare at, and leaves a soft white powder. Weigh it, and the powder is heavier than the ribbon was. 2,4 grams of magnesium becomes 4,0 grams of powder. Where did the extra come from? The air. Every magnesium atom grabbed an oxygen atom and became magnesium oxide. Two magnesium plus one oxygen molecule gives two magnesium oxide. Steel wool does the same, spraying orange sparks as iron grabs oxygen to make iron oxide, and its side of a balance drops. The rule for every metal is simple: metal plus oxygen gives metal oxide, and the oxide always weighs more.
visual_style: Magnesium ribbon flaring white against a dark background; a digital scale ticking upward; oxygen atoms snapping onto magnesium atoms; steel wool sparkling on a balance that tips.
pacing: Fast contrast at the start, a pause at the reveal, a quick sparkling finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write the balanced equation for iron yourself.
